explanation: Heating cinnabar (mercury sulphide ore) in air converts it to mercuric oxide, releasing sulphur dioxide gas — the first step in extracting mercury, a metal unreactive enough to be obtained by heating alone.

beaker_view.final_appearance: A reddish residue of mercuric oxide.
beaker_view.observation: Heated strongly in air, the brick-red ore gives off choking fumes and leaves behind a reddish residue.
